Oversized containers

Translating a long document is mostly a scheduling problem. A model produces a bounded number of tokens per second, so one enormous paragraph becomes one enormous wait. The renderer can only show a translation after it has been produced, which means the segmenter decides how long the reader stares at the original text. Cutting an oversized container into several blocks changes the shape of that wait: each block is short, so the first one comes back quickly and the page starts filling in immediately instead of waiting for the slowest chunk of the entire document. A second consideration is cost. Every block carries its own envelope, its own copy of the shared context, and its own entry in the batch. Splitting everything down to single sentences would multiply the prompt overhead without improving the reading experience, so the threshold has to stay high enough that ordinary paragraphs are left alone, and only the containers that are clearly too long for a single response get divided. Finally there is restoring the original text. Every translation must be reversible byte for byte, which rules out cutting inside a text node: a node that has been split can never be reassembled with the same object identity. Cutting between child nodes keeps every original node intact, so restore can put the exact same objects back where they came from, and the page returns to precisely the DOM it had before the translation ran.

This nested paragraph belongs to its own block, not to the container.

A container that mixes prose with block level descendants cannot be divided safely, because the pieces would no longer be a contiguous run inside the container and restoring them would land in the wrong place. The safe answer is to leave such a container alone: it stays one block, however long it happens to be, and the reader waits a little longer for it. That is an acceptable trade because the common case on documentation sites is a flat run of prose with inline links and emphasis, and that case is exactly the one worth cutting apart. Keeping the rule this narrow also keeps the renderer simple, since every segment it handles is guaranteed to be a contiguous slice of the original children. There is a second reason to be careful with containers that hold block level descendants. The block below belongs to its own translation unit, so the surrounding prose is only part of what the container displays, and the reader sees the two pieces arrive at different times no matter what the splitter does. Dividing the prose as well would add a third arrival time without buying anything, and it would mix two restore strategies in one container, which is precisely the sort of interaction that breaks in ways nobody notices until a page fails to restore.
Table cells are rendered differently in bilingual mode, where the translation is appended inside the cell rather than after the container, so dividing a cell into several segments would need a second rendering path and a second set of restore rules. Rather than carry that duplication for a case that barely happens, the splitter simply declines to touch table cells. The cost of that decision is bounded and easy to reason about, which matters more here than shaving a few seconds off a rare page. A cell is also a poor unit for splitting in the first place. Its width is usually narrow, the text inside it is short by construction, and the column already gives the reader a visual signal that the content is a single field rather than a paragraph. Dividing one would stack several translated fragments inside the same cell, which reads worse than the single block the reader gets today, and it would leave the restore path with two different rules to remember for a shape of content that is genuinely rare on the pages this tool is built for.

Short paragraphs are never divided.
